title: DNS Extensions to Support IP Version 6
summary: Defines the changes the Domain Name System needs so that hosts running IPv6 can be found by name. It introduces a new record type for IPv6 addresses and a way to look up a name from an IPv6 address. It was replaced by RFC 3596.

eli5.summary: The phone book only had room for short old-style numbers. This added a new kind of entry for the much longer new numbers, so you can still look up a friend by name.

questions: what is the aaaa record type number
subtitle: How the Domain Name System first learned to store and look up IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: DNS applications assume that address queries return 32-bit IPv4 addresses, so IPv6 addresses could not easily be stored.
tldr.mechanism: A new AAAA record type (type 28) holds a 128-bit address, the IP6.INT domain handles address-to-name lookups, and NS, MX and MB queries now add both A and AAAA records to the additional section.
tldr.outcome: This Proposed Standard has been obsoleted by RFC 3596 and updated by RFC 2874 and RFC 3152.

facts.label: Queries returning A and AAAA extras

today: RFC 1886 was a Proposed Standard but is obsoleted by RFC 3596, and it is also updated by RFC 2874 and RFC 3152. Read RFC 3596 for the current definition.

sections.title: Why DNS Needed Changes
sections.content:
Existing DNS support for storing Internet addresses cannot easily be extended to IPv6, since applications assume that address queries return 32-bit IPv4 addresses only. This memo defines three extensions: a new resource record type that maps a name to an IPv6 address, a new domain for lookups based on address, and redefined queries that locate both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses in additional section processing.

The changes are designed to be compatible with existing software, and existing IPv4 support is retained. The coexistence of IPv4 and IPv6 in DNS is left to a separate transition document.
sections.eli5: The old phone book had boxes sized for short numbers. The new numbers are much longer, so the book needed a new kind of box without breaking the old ones.

sections.title: The AAAA Record
sections.content:
The AAAA resource record type is specific to the Internet class and stores a single IPv6 address. Its type value is 28 (decimal). A host with more than one IPv6 address must have more than one such record.

The 128-bit address is encoded in the data portion in network byte order, high-order byte first. In a master database file, it is written in the textual form of an IPv6 address defined in RFC 1884.

An AAAA query for a domain name in the Internet class returns all associated AAAA records in the answer section. A type AAAA query does not perform additional section processing.
sections.eli5: An AAAA entry is one line in the phone book that holds one long new-style number. If a computer has several numbers, it gets several lines.

sections.title: Looking Up a Name from an Address
sections.content:
A special domain rooted at IP6.INT maps an IPv6 address to a host name, although it may be used for other purposes as well. An address becomes a name by writing its nibbles (4-bit hexadecimal digits) in reverse order, low-order nibble first, separated by dots, with the suffix .IP6.INT.

The RFC's example is the address 4321:0:1:2:3:4:567:89ab, whose lookup name is shown below.
sections.eli5: To look up who owns a number, you write the number backwards one digit at a time and add a special ending. Then you ask the phone book about that backwards name.

sections.title: Changes to Existing Queries
sections.content:
Existing query types that perform type A additional section processing, namely name server (NS), mail exchange (MX) and mailbox (MB), must be redefined to perform both type A and type AAAA additional section processing.

So when a name server answers one of these queries, it must add any relevant IPv4 addresses and any relevant IPv6 addresses it has locally to the additional section of the response.

The memo says security issues are not discussed in it.
sections.eli5: When the phone book tells you where a mail office is, it now also hands you both the old-style and the new-style numbers if it has them.
